title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning Alignment Science Blog Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning Paul Rosu October 15, 2026 Rowan Wang tl;dr We train LLM alignment auditors with reinforcement learning. In our training environment, the policy investigates target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. After finetuning Haiku 4.5 on this environment, it matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and generalizes to harder, fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold. 📄 Paper , 💻 Code Introduction Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations ( Anthropic, 2025 ). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri ( Fronsdal et al., 2025 ), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations ( Kissane et al., 2026 ), and AuditBench ( Sheshadri et al., 2026 ) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models. We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). title: Learning Speech Attribute Representations via Multi-Teacher Distillation
summary: Recent post-training approaches have shown that self-supervised speech encoders can be adapted to learn a single utterance-level speech attribute through knowledge distillation. In this work, we investigate whether a single speech encoder can simultaneously preserve multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations. We propose a multi-attribute multi-teacher distillation framework that learns semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four frozen teacher models using a shared SSL backbone and attribute-specific branches. Experiments on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and speech emotion recognition show that the proposed model achieves performance close to dedicated single-task students while requiring only a single shared encoder. Furthermore, the learned layer aggregation strategies reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different depths of the SSL encoder, providing new insights into the organization of speech representations.
